findings.title: Detach background writes from request cancellation
findings.body: The asynchronous legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context. HTTP request contexts are canceled when the handler returns, so returning the unified-storage result can cancel the legacy write before it starts or while it is running; the ten-second timeout does not prevent parent cancellation. The same problem affects Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Preserve the necessary context values but detach cancellation before applying the background timeout so successful requests actually replicate to legacy storage.

findings.title: Preserve write ordering when replicating asynchronously
findings.body: Each successful mutation launches an independent goroutine with no ordering between legacy operations. Even sequential client requests can therefore be applied out of order: a create followed by a delete can execute the legacy delete first and then leave the deleted object present in legacy, while two updates can leave the older value last. Since legacy is intended as a safety copy, replication needs an ordered mechanism for conflicting writes rather than independent goroutines.

findings.title: Replicate the committed update result instead of replaying objInfo
findings.body: The legacy Update now receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the updateWrapper containing the object committed by unified storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a PATCH or server-side apply transformation that depends on the existing object. Re-evaluating it against legacy's potentially stale object can produce a different result—for example, preserving fields that an earlier unified update changed but that have not yet reached legacy. Pass a snapshot of the successful unified update result through the wrapper so legacy receives the same desired object rather than recomputing the request against a different base.

findings.title: Do not use object names as the metric kind label
findings.body: The successful Delete metric passes name where the other duration calls pass options.Kind. This creates a separate Prometheus label value for every deleted object instead of a bounded resource kind, causing unbounded metric-series growth as objects are deleted and making successful and failed delete metrics inconsistent. Pass options.Kind here.

findings.title: Attribute operation durations to the store that was called
findings.body: DeleteCollection records its asynchronous legacy operation with recordStorageDuration, so legacy latency and errors are reported as unified-storage observations. Conversely, the Create and Update unified-storage error paths at lines 45 and 129 call recordLegacyDuration even though legacy is not called. These mistakes hide failures in the actual store and incorrectly inflate the other store's metrics. Use recordLegacyDuration for the legacy collection deletion and recordStorageDuration for unified Create/Update failures.
